Your first day in the kitchen
Today is your trial day at a restaurant. The chef has called you to the counter.
Chef: "First tell me, what's the first thing you do when you enter the kitchen?"
I put on my apron and hairnet and wash my hands
Every job in the kitchen starts with cleanliness. Hair is covered, hands are washed with soap.
I grab a knife and start chopping right away
Unwashed hands carry germs onto food. Hygiene first.
I walk around tasting the dishes
Tasting is done with the chef's permission and a clean spoon.
Chef: "You're going to chop these onions. How do you hold the knife and the onion?"
I curl my fingertips in and rest the knife against my knuckles
This is called the claw grip. Your fingertips stay away from the blade.
I keep my fingers straight and grip the onion tightly
Straight fingers are in the knife's path; the risk of cutting yourself is high.
I hold the onion in my hand and cut it in the air
Cutting is always done on a steady board.
The knife slips from your hand and is falling. What do you do?
I step back and let it fall
Never try to catch a falling knife. Pick it up afterwards and wash it.
I try to catch it in mid-air
One of the most dangerous kitchen accidents. Let the knife go, let it fall.
I try to stop it with my foot
A foot gets injured just as easily as a hand.

Hygiene and food safety
Handwashing
Hands are washed with soap for at least 20 seconds and dried with a single-use paper towel. Always after the toilet, raw meat and rubbish.
personal hygiene
The danger zone
Germs multiply fastest between about 5 °C and 63 °C. Food is not left in this range for long.
danger zone
Cold chain
The fridge is kept at 0–4 °C, the freezer at −18 °C or below. Thawing is done in the fridge, not on the counter.
cold chain
Hot holding
Hot food ready for service is kept above 63 °C. Reheated food must be heated thoroughly all the way through, and only once.
hot holding
Cross-contamination
Raw meat and cooked or ready-to-eat food are never prepared on the same board with the same knife. In the fridge, raw meat goes on the bottom shelf.
cross-contamination
Hygiene certificate
In Türkiye, people working in restaurant kitchens must receive hygiene training under the Hygiene Training Regulation.
hygiene training

Make lentil soup
The chef wants lentil soup for lunch service. Do the steps in the right order.
Wash your hands, weigh the ingredients and lay them out on the counter

Before anything else, hygiene and preparation.
Pick over the lentils and rinse until the water runs clear
Stones and grit are removed, and surface starch and dust are washed away.

First, a flavour base is made in the pot.

Fluffy rice pilaf
Rice pilaf is the most ordered dish in a lokanta. Make rice pilaf in the right order.
Wash the rice, soak it in warm salted water and drain
Surface starch is removed so the grains don't stick or break.
Before the stove: the rice itself.
Melt the butter in the pot
The rice will be toasted in hot fat.
The pot is heating; what goes in first?
Add the rice and toast until the grains turn translucent
Toasting coats each grain in fat so it stays separate.
The fat is ready; now the rice.
Add the measured hot water and the salt
The amount of water depends on the rice and is in the recipe; hot water doesn't stop the cooking.
The toasted rice needs liquid.
Once boiling, cook covered on low heat without stirring until the water is absorbed
Stirring breaks the grains and makes it mushy.
Water's in; now patience.
Take it off the heat and let it rest with a clean cloth under the lid
The cloth absorbs steam; the grains settle in their own steam.
The water is gone, but the pilaf isn't ready to serve yet.
Gently fluff the pilaf before serving
Separate grains and the right texture come just before serving.
The final touch.
The secret of pilaf
Wash and soak: get rid of the starch.
Toast, then add hot water.
Don't stir while it cooks.

Kitchen safety
Kitchen accidents happen in a moment of carelessness. Tap each action: right or wrong?
Right
Wrong
Walking with the knife point down and calling "Knife behind!"
Everyone in a kitchen is moving; a warning prevents collisions.
Dropping a knife into soapy dishwater
A knife under the water is invisible; whoever reaches in gets cut. Wash knives separately.
Leaving pan handles sticking out over the edge of the stove
If someone bumps the handle, boiling food spills. Turn handles inward.
Holding a hot tray with a wet cloth
A wet cloth conducts heat at once and the steam scalds. Use a dry cloth or oven glove.
Holding a burn under cool running water for at least 10 minutes
Cool water stops the burn from going deeper. For large or serious burns, call 112.
Putting toothpaste or yogurt on a burn
It traps heat and risks infection. Put nothing but water on a burn.
Pressing a cut with a clean cloth, bandaging it and working with a glove
The bleeding stops and the wound doesn't touch food. Deep cuts need medical care.
Wiping up spilled oil at once and marking the floor with a warning sign
An oily floor is the most common cause of slips in a kitchen.
Lifting a heavy sack of flour by bending at the waist
Squat at the knees and keep the load close to your body; if it's too heavy, ask for help.
Putting a damp cloth under the board while chopping
A sliding board is the most common reason a knife slips onto a hand.
A safe kitchen
Knives: point down, call out, wash separately.
Handles inward, dry cloth for hot pans.
Burns: cool running water; no toothpaste, no yogurt.
Keep floors dry, lift with your knees.
Busy lunch service
12:30, the dining room is full. The chef has put you on the soup and salad section.
You now need to chop tomatoes for a salad on the board where you just cut raw chicken. What do you do?
I take a separate, clean board and knife

Wiping doesn't remove germs; the board must be washed and disinfected or swapped.
I flip the board over and chop on the other side
Chicken juices may have got underneath too; the risk remains.
Waiter: "There's a customer with a peanut allergy at table 3. Is the salad safe?"
I check the ingredients and dressing in the recipe and ask the chef
Allergen questions are answered by checking the recipe and the chef, not by guessing.
I say "I don't see any peanuts, it's safe"
There may be hidden allergens in the dressing or garnish. Looking isn't enough.
I pick out the peanuts by hand and send it out
Picking them out doesn't remove contamination; the dish must be made from scratch with clean tools.
You check the soup pot: the temperature is 50 °C. Service is still going.
I bring the soup back to the boil, then keep it above 63 °C
50 °C is in the danger zone. It must be reheated thoroughly and kept hot.
It's fine a bit warm, so customers don't get burnt
Lukewarm soup stays in the range where germs multiply fastest.
I add hot water to it and carry on serving
The texture is ruined and the whole soup still doesn't get hot enough.
Service rules
Separate boards and knives for raw and cooked.

Cooking methods
Dry heat
Cooking without water, using hot air, fat or fire: grilling, roasting, sautéing, frying.
dry heat
Moist heat
Cooking with water or steam: boiling, steaming, poaching.
moist heat
Combination method
First seared over high heat, then cooked slowly with a little liquid under a lid. Tough meats become tender.
braising
The browning reaction
When meat and vegetables brown over high heat, new flavours and aromas form. Ingredients don't go in until the pan is properly hot.
Maillard reaction
Poaching
Cooking gently in water that is barely trembling, not boiling. For eggs and fish.
poaching
Thermometer
Whether meat is cooked is judged by measuring its core temperature, not by eye. The inside of chicken and minced meat must reach at least 75 °C.
core temperature

The gauge is rising. Press STOP when it enters the target range. Too early or too late and the food is ruined.

Dinner service

You put meat in the pan but the pan wasn't hot enough; the meat isn't browning and is releasing its juices. What do you do?
